note: FR-LOC-002: 'Formatting follows the administration's locale, not the user's UI language, so
amounts read identically to every user.' Every user includes a user reading a PDF the API
rendered, so there are TWO implementations of this formatting - packages/i18n/src/format.ts
and apps/api/src/api/i18n/formatting.py - and 'identically' is a claim about both.
This table is what makes the claim checkable. packages/i18n/src/format.test.ts and
apps/api/tests/i18n/test_formatting.py each run every case here against their own
implementation, so a divergence is a failure in both suites rather than a difference nobody
notices until a Dutch invoice shows 1,234.56. The same device migration 0029 uses for the
fiscal period derivation, which also exists twice (SQL and Python) and is compared against a
The space after the currency symbol is U+00A0, a NON-BREAKING space, which is what CLDR
nl-NL specifies and what stops '€' and '1.234,56' landing on two lines of an invoice. It is
a literal character in this file and therefore invisible in a diff, so neither implementation
types it: both take it from a named field on the locale spec, and the cases here are what
would catch one of them reverting to U+0020.

money.note: The first grouping boundary. Off-by-one grouping bugs live here.
CLDR nl-NL's currency pattern is '¤ #,##0.00;¤ -#,##0.00' - the sign sits after the symbol, not before it. Getting this backwards produces '-€ 1.234,56', which reads as English.
A scale-1 input is padded, not rejected: '10.5' is an exact decimal that happens to have been written short. It is losing digits that is forbidden, not having fewer.
numeric(19,2)'s ceiling: 17 integer digits. Formatting must not route through a float on the way - 2^53 is exhausted around 9.0e15, four digits below this.

The float trap made explicit: 4335.09 + 2964.61 is 7299.700000000001 in binary floating point (api.ledger.model's docstring names this exact sum). The formatter is handed the decimal sum and must print it.
Negative zero is not a thing a ledger produces, and an implementation that formats the sign from a numeric comparison could still emit it.

number.note: A bare number takes the sign directly before its digits - unlike the currency pattern above, where the symbol comes first.
A BTW rate. Scale 0, so no decimal separator at all: '21%' not '21,00%'.
Four-digit years and quantities are grouped in nl-NL. That is correct for a quantity and wrong for a year, which is why a year is a DATE and never goes through this function.

date.note: The machine-readable style. Locale-independent by construction - the same argument ledger.money_text (migration 0023) makes for using '.' rather than the locale's decimal separator in a report a consumer parses.
Long style drops the leading zero on the day; short style keeps it, because a fixed-width date is what makes a column of them scannable.
Dutch month names are lower case mid-sentence and standalone. Capitalising them is an English habit.

note: Inputs both implementations must REFUSE rather than render. Every one of them is a way a
wrong number reaches a screen looking right, so a formatter that silently coped would be
hiding the bug rather than the bug being visible (CLAUDE.md rule four).

money.why: more precision than a posted amount has. Rounding it here would print a number that is not the number in the ledger.
already formatted, in some other locale. Reformatting it would parse the comma as a decimal point or drop it.
already formatted, in this locale. Same trap, arriving from a round trip through the UI.
exponent notation. Accepting it means accepting whatever produced it, which was floating point.
not a decimal literal - and the leading zero is what keeps a small amount readable.
empty. A missing amount must render as absent, never as zero.
whitespace. Trimming silently would let a padded field through unnoticed.
an explicit plus sign is not something this system produces; accepting it means accepting a foreign format.

date.why: not ISO 8601 - unpadded, so a string sort over these would be wrong.
already formatted for nl-NL. Re-parsing it as ISO would silently read year 2.
a day that does not exist in that month. Rolling it forward to 1 March is what a lenient parser does, and it is how a period boundary moves by a day.
a timestamp. A posting date is a date; carrying a time invites a timezone to change it.
